en: Advayavajra’s Works 15. *Yuganaddhaprakāśa*,
edited by Mahāmahopādhyāya Hara Prasad Shastri.
In the *Advayavajrasaṃgraha* (GOS 1927, Baroda),
edited by the Mikkyō Seiten Kenkyūkai;
and in the *Annual Report of the Institute for Comprehensive Studies of Buddhism, Taishō University*.
Whatever manifestation there may be, that is pure; if it is awakened, it is changelessness.
A transformation arises through conditions, yet those conditions also [arise] through them; thus, there is no arising.
Form does not exist within form, nor does it exist within the eye; nor does it exist within the consciousness produced by them, just like the analogy of fire in wood. (2)
Whether in the churning vessel or in the hands of the person, fire does not exist as something pre-established; it arises through dependence upon its conditions.
Is delusion first produced toward one's own sons, or is it produced toward a son?
If it is only toward a son and not first toward others, then that [delusion] lacks the nature of a real entity.
Thus, because phenomena are mere conditions, they lack intrinsic nature;
dwelling in that very state, the yogi does not transgress the vow. (5)
Neither loss nor gain exists in all cases, yet conventional discourse continues;
like an illusion, this [world] is devoid of intrinsic nature, through the realization of dependent origination. (6)
Because of the absence of intrinsic nature, there is non-arising; because of dependence on conditions, there is non-cessation.
Therefore, existence and non-existence do not exist; rather, it appears as the yoke of union.
The unity of emptiness and compassion must be practiced, not through one's own conceptual construction;
for emptiness and luminosity are, by their very nature, conjoined in union.

The practitioner of excellent yoga should directly realize his own emptiness, which is vast, profound, and endowed with the excellence of all aspects, and should thereby perform worship to the Buddhas.
The wise one, always established in body, mind, and speech, may either engage in conduct or not; he is called a practitioner of conduct (caryācārī). 10.
The Illumination of the Union is completed.
Farewell.
